title: Al-Fatiha: The Opening
intro: Seven days through Al-Fatiha, the opening surah of the Quran, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: This account shares one verse of the Quran a day, read in order through a surah, with a little context. We begin with Al-Fatiha, "The Opening": seven verses at the heart of every daily prayer. In the common numbering its first verse is the Bismillah, which also opens every surah but one. "Beneficent" and "Merciful" both come from r-h-m, the Arabic root for mercy.

posts.display: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.
posts.caption: Al-hamdu lillah, "praise be to Allah", is among the phrases Muslims say most often: after a meal, after sneezing, or when asked how they are. "Lord" translates Rabb, which carries the sense of one who nurtures and sustains. "The Worlds" means every realm of creation.

The two names of mercy from the Bismillah return here: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim. Many commentators explain Ar-Rahman as mercy vast enough to embrace all creation, and Ar-Rahim as mercy that is enduring and given in particular. Before Al-Fatiha mentions judgment, it mentions mercy twice.

posts.display: Master of the Day of Judgment.
posts.caption: "The Day of Judgment" is Yawm ad-Din. Here din means reckoning or recompense, though elsewhere it often means religion. The Arabic on screen reads Māliki, "Master" or "Owner"; another of the accepted recitations reads Maliki, "King".

Here the surah turns from speaking about Allah to speaking to Him directly. In Arabic, "Thee" comes first in both phrases, which gives the sense of "Thee alone" that Pickthall marks in brackets. Worship and asking for help sit side by side. In a hadith qudsi recorded in Sahih Muslim, Allah calls this verse the one that is "between Me and My servant".

With this verse the prayer becomes a request. Sirat means a road or path, and mustaqim means straight or upright. Muslims make this request many times a day, and commentators explain that even the guided keep asking: to stay on the path and be led further along it.

The request ends by describing the path: the way of those Allah has favoured, not of those who earned anger or went astray. Commentators link the favoured to An-Nisa 4:69, which names the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. That completes Al-Fatiha, seven short verses that Muslims around the world know by heart.
